papers.title: DISTRIBUTED SWARM INTELLIGENCE FOR AUTONOMOUS VEHICLE MORPHOLOGY AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:分散式群體智慧與自主車體決策極限 24/90 DISTRIBUTED SWARM INTELLIGENCE FOR AUTONOMOUS VEHICLE MORPHOLOGY AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page high-density English Research Working Edition within the STARLI YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy (Research Institute XXXVI, Flagship 24 of 90). It examines whether many locally deciding robotic modules can produce a predictable, structurally qualified global body shape without surrendering load-transfer integrity, explicit human stop authority, module identity or full resource accounting. Its three-way coupling is Swarm Intelligence x Local Decision-Making x Global Safety. Tests are proposed only for unoccupied scaled panels, connector coupons, an instrumented 24-module structure and hardware-in-the-loop environments. This is a hypothesis-forming research design, not a claimed roadworthy vehicle, passenger safety achievement or nanoscale-to-macroscale engineering demonstration. The preregistered candidate asks whether, under the same material, energy, computation, sensing, communication, operator and mission budgets, a frozen distributed morphology policy improves deadline-valid packet survival without worsening full-cycle mission energy. More importantly, it may not violate even one preregistered mechanical or physical stop invariant. Strong competitors are tuned centralized predictive control, passive safe-hold modules, an ordinary local rule, and learned controllers protected by an equivalent independent safety shield. Concealed tests include false-status agents, split-brain groups, under-preloaded latches, weak-mode structural instability, old membership epochs, actuator saturation, unmetered field energy and false software stop acknowledgements. Energy per transition is E_tr = integral_0^T (P_act + P_sense + P_compute + P_comm) dt; cooling, reset work and other external sources remain separately accountable rather than disappearing from the ledger. Thirty distinct mathematical research plates range across distributed consensus, physical degrees of freedom, stiffness and rigidity rank, safe viability, control barrier inequalities, robust action filters, reachable sets, causal policy identification, worst-tail risk, energy and thermal budgets, correlated measurement uncertainty, temporal authorization and conjunctive qualification. Each gives its governing construction, units and limits, a concrete blind refutation and links to related investigations. The treatment distinguishes mathematical guarantees conditional on assumptions from evidence about real machinery. Eighty-two chapters contain 410 separately paginated investigations spanning local policy and voting, physical load-bearing morphology, sensing and learning under uncertainty, global safety vetoes, fair causal baselines and cross-generation requalification. The 200 Research Gates carry independently identified failures, competing accounts, physical stop conditions and successor evidence packets; they are research invitations rather than completed results. Thirty-three distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos propose different physical instruments, calibration objects, safety-gate demonstrators and independent refusal replayers. The complete work preserves failed trials and abstentions instead of silently excluding them. This work is restricted to prospective non-occupancy engineering and makes no road-certification, crash-protection or full-sized autonomous vehicle claim. Relevant methodological evidence includes Robo-Matter (DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6), flying-swarm shape assembly (10.1038/s44172-026-00715-3), adaptive magnetic microrobots (10.1038/s41427-026-00682-3), safe multi-robot control review (10.1016/j.arcontrol.2024.100948), distributed control-barrier safety (10.1109/LRA.2024.3414268), changing-topology consensus (10.1109/TAC.2005.846556), and multi-agent adaptive safety (10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10611037). The supplied Flagship 13 ancestor identifiers are 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839; their public metadata were not independently verified in this edition. Cited external research supports component theories or methods, not this integrated F24 concept. Methodological DOI context includes Robo-Matter (10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6), flying-swarm shape assembly (10.1038/s44172-026-00715-3), real-time scheduling (10.1145/321738.321743), battery SOC estimation (10.1038/s44359-026-00145-6), modular reconfiguration (10.1007/s10846-024-02067-6) and dynamic topology consensus (10.1109/TAC.2005.846556), alongside author-supplied Flagship 13 research ancestry (10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839; metadata not independently confirmed here). A wired centralized architecture and an optimized safe-hold controller form strong rivals. Important refutations include a hidden radio partition, a stale but successfully delivered sensor value, an unmetered field-driven repeater, a swapped physical module ID, a false software acknowledgement or failure of real physical cessation. The source contract's heat-balance equation rho*c_p*dT/dt = div(k grad T) + qdot is retained as a powered-node thermal constraint, not presented as a communication theorem. Relevant external research includes Robo-Matter (10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6), flying-swarm shape assembly (10.1038/s44172-026-00715-3), adaptive magnetic microrobots (10.1038/s41427-026-00682-3), consensus and cooperation (10.1109/JPROC.2006.887293), consensus under changing topologies (10.1109/TAC.2005.846556) and networked control under packet delay and loss (10.1080/23307706.2026.2683639). papers.summary: Hybrid model predictive control with both continuous and discrete variables is widely applicable to robotic control tasks, especially those involving contacts with the environment. papers.summary: The misuse of deepfake technology against public figures on social media presents significant challenges for criminal law enforcement in Indonesia, particularly concerning the protection of personal rights, reputation, and digital identity. papers.title: ParaDiGM: Parallel Distributed General Mesh
papers.summary: ParaDiGM (Parallel Distributed General Mesh) is an open-source C library (LGPL) designed to overcome the technological bottlenecks associated with geometric data handling and mesh manipulation in massively parallel numerical simulations.Originally developed as the geometric engine for the CWIPI coupling library (Quémerais et al., 2026), it has evolved into a standalone infrastructure designed to manage distributed meshes at the billion-element scale and beyond.
